prompt: `except LookupError` catches which of these?
hint: Catching a class catches everything below it.

choices.text: A `KeyError`
choices.why: Right — and an `IndexError`, which is its sibling.

choices.text: A `FileNotFoundError`
choices.why: That is under `OSError`.

choices.text: A `ValueError`
choices.why: That sits elsewhere in the tree.

choices.text: Every exception there is
choices.why: That would be `BaseException`.

prompt: Why do `SystemExit` and `KeyboardInterrupt` sit outside `Exception`?
hint: They are not the program going wrong.

choices.text: They are raised by the operating system rather than by Python
choices.why: Python raises both of them.

choices.text: They cannot be caught at all
choices.why: They can, which is the hazard.

choices.text: They are somebody asking the program to stop
choices.why: Right — which is why `except Exception` leaves them alone.

choices.text: They are older than the `Exception` class
choices.why: Age is not what the tree records.

prompt: What breaks when you write a bare `except:` inside a loop?
hint: Press the keys and see.

choices.text: The traceback is printed twice
choices.why: Nothing is printed at all, which is the other complaint.

choices.text: `Ctrl-C` stops working
choices.why: Right — the interrupt is an exception and the clause caught it.

choices.text: Nothing; a bare `except` is the same as `except Exception`
choices.why: It is wider by exactly the two classes that matter here.

choices.text: The loop runs one extra time
choices.why: The count is unaffected.

prompt: Where does `except Exception` belong?
hint: Once, and at one end.

choices.text: At the top of a program, to log and exit non-zero
choices.why: Right — everywhere else it is a net over code you have not read.

choices.text: Nowhere; it is always wrong
choices.why: It has one correct home, which is the top.

choices.text: Around every call that touches a file, since the filesystem is the unreliable part
choices.why: Name the file errors instead.

choices.text: Inside every function, so that nothing ever escapes to a traceback
choices.why: Then nothing ever reaches a traceback.

prompt: An exception object carries three things. Which three?
hint: One says what kind, one says which, one says where.

choices.text: The message, the time and the thread
choices.why: Nothing records a time.

choices.text: The class, the message and the traceback
choices.why: Right — and a log wants all three, because none of them is enough alone.

choices.text: The class, the message and the handler that caught it
choices.why: Nothing records who caught it.

choices.text: The class, the line number and the file
choices.why: Two of those are inside the traceback.

prompt: A `try` around three statements catches a `KeyError`. What is the risk?
hint: Which of the three raised it?

choices.text: The other two statements run anyway
choices.why: They do not; the block is abandoned.

choices.text: Python only reports the first statement's failure
choices.why: It reports whichever one raised.

choices.text: `KeyError` cannot be caught from more than one statement
choices.why: It can, which is the problem.

choices.text: The one you caught might not be the one you meant
choices.why: Right — and the handler cannot tell the difference.

prompt: Clauses are tried in order. What does a base class above a subclass make the second clause?
hint: It never gets a turn.

choices.text: Dead code
choices.why: Right — and nothing warns you about it.

choices.text: Faster, because the common case is first
choices.why: It is not reached at all, so speed is moot.

choices.text: A second handler for the same failure
choices.why: The second one is never reached.

choices.text: A syntax error
choices.why: Python accepts it.

prompt: What are the two good reasons to catch an exception?
hint: Say something better, or do something else.

choices.text: The exception is slow, and the traceback is long
choices.why: Neither is a reason to catch anything.

choices.text: You have an alternative, or you have something clearer to say about the failure
choices.why: Right — and "because it might fail" is not one of them.

choices.text: A library asked you to in its documentation, and the linter suggested it as well
choices.why: Neither knows what you would do about it.

choices.text: The code below must keep running, and the log must stay clean of anything alarming
choices.why: A log that stays clean through a failure is the problem, not the goal.

prompt: `except Exception: pass` says what?
hint: Two lines, and a decision inside them.

choices.text: Retry the block from the beginning
choices.why: Nothing retries.

choices.text: This failure has already been logged elsewhere
choices.why: Nothing logged it.

choices.text: Something went wrong and nobody needs to know
choices.why: Right — and if it really is safe, a comment says which class and why.

choices.text: Re-raise after the handler finishes
choices.why: That is a bare `raise`, which is not there.

prompt: Catch two unrelated classes in one clause: `except ______ValueError, TypeError):`
hint: One character.

prompt: What does the `else` clause of a `try` do?
hint: It is about the case where nothing failed.

choices.text: Runs instead of the `try` on a second attempt
choices.why: Nothing retries.

choices.text: Runs when no `except` clause matched
choices.why: That exception propagates instead.

choices.text: Runs before the `try`, to set things up
choices.why: Nothing runs before.

choices.text: Runs when the `try` did not raise
choices.why: Right — which is how the `try` stays one line long.

prompt: Why put `save(value)` in the `else` rather than at the end of the `try`?
hint: The net is the problem.

choices.text: A failure inside `save` is then not caught by the handler above
choices.why: Right — otherwise the handler answers for the wrong failure.

choices.text: `save` would otherwise run even on failure, writing a value that was never parsed
choices.why: It would not run at all.

choices.text: `save` runs faster outside the `try`, because the block costs something to enter
choices.why: The cost of a `try` that does not raise is nothing.

choices.text: The `try` may only hold one statement
choices.why: It may hold as many as you like.

prompt: When does `finally` run?
hint: Count the ways out of the block.

choices.text: On every path out — success, handled, unhandled, and a `return`
choices.why: Right — which is what makes it the place for cleanup.

choices.text: Only when no exception was raised
choices.why: That is the `else`.

choices.text: After the whole function returns, like a callback registered at the end of it
choices.why: It runs as the block is left.

choices.text: Only when an exception was raised and no clause above it matched the class
choices.why: It runs on success too.

prompt: Is `try`/`finally` with no `except` a normal thing to write?
hint: It says two things at once.

choices.text: No, `except` is required by the syntax
choices.why: Either `except` or `finally` is enough.

choices.text: No, because with no `except` the exception is swallowed on the way out silently
choices.why: The exception continues on its way.

choices.text: Yes, and it quietly catches everything as a side effect of having no `except`
choices.why: It catches nothing.

choices.text: Yes — I am not handling this, and I am still tidying up
choices.why: Right — and `with` is the one-line version of exactly that.

prompt: `try: return compute()` with `finally: return fallback()`. What comes back?
hint: One of the two returns wins.

choices.text: `fallback()`
choices.why: Right — the `finally`'s return replaces the one on its way out, exception included.

choices.text: `compute()`
choices.why: It was on its way out and got replaced.

choices.text: Both, as a tuple
choices.why: Only one value leaves a function.

choices.text: A `SyntaxError`, because two returns conflict
choices.why: It is legal, which is why the rule has to be a habit.

prompt: `int(raw)` where `raw` is a word. Which class should YOUR wrapper raise?
hint: The type was right and the value was not.

choices.text: `TypeError`
choices.why: The type of `raw` was fine; it was a string as expected.

choices.text: `Exception`
choices.why: A caller could only catch that by catching everything.

choices.text: `ValueError`
choices.why: Right — and the message names the file, the field and the value.

choices.text: `KeyError`
choices.why: Nothing was looked up.

prompt: What is wrong with `raise Exception("something went wrong")`?
hint: Think about the caller.

choices.text: It is slower than a specific class, because the base has more subclasses to test
choices.why: The cost is identical.

choices.text: Python forbids raising `Exception` directly, so a subclass is the only option
choices.why: It permits it.

choices.text: Nothing catches it except a clause that catches everything
choices.why: Right — which is the situation this lesson is trying to avoid.

choices.text: The traceback is shorter
choices.why: The traceback is the same.

prompt: Which message is the useful one?
hint: Somebody is reading it in a log at three in the morning.

choices.text: `error in line 42`
choices.why: The line of whose file, and what was wrong with it?

choices.text: `ValueError`
choices.why: That is the class, which the log already prints.

choices.text: `config.toml: port must be a number, not '8o80'`
choices.why: Right — which file, which field, what was there, what was expected.

choices.text: `invalid config`
choices.why: It names nothing anybody can act on.

prompt: `raise ConfigError(...) from e` differs from the same line without `from e` how?
hint: The traceback says something different between the two.

choices.text: It suppresses the traceback of both
choices.why: Both are printed either way.

choices.text: It says the first was the direct cause, rather than an accident during handling
choices.why: Right — and `from None` hides the original entirely.

choices.text: It discards the original exception, leaving the traceback with only the new one
choices.why: That is `from None`.

choices.text: It re-raises the original instead of the new one, so the caller sees the low-level class
choices.why: The new one is what propagates.

prompt: A bare `raise` inside a handler does what?
hint: Nothing new is made.

choices.text: Raises `RuntimeError`
choices.why: That is what a bare `raise` outside a handler does.

choices.text: Ends the function and returns `None`, the way a bare `return` would have done
choices.why: The exception continues upwards.

choices.text: Raises a new exception of the same class, with a traceback starting here
choices.why: Nothing is constructed.

choices.text: Re-raises what you caught, with its original traceback
choices.why: Right — and `raise e` would truncate that traceback.

prompt: What is the whole definition of an exception class of your own?
hint: It needs no body.

choices.text: `class ConfigError(Exception):` and a docstring
choices.why: Right — inheriting `Exception` is the entire mechanism.

choices.text: A subclass of `BaseException` with a message argument
choices.why: `BaseException` is the one to stay away from, beside `KeyboardInterrupt`.

choices.text: A function that returns an `Exception` instance with your text in it
choices.why: An exception is a class, and raising an instance of `Exception` is the thing to avoid.

choices.text: A class with `__init__`, `__str__` and a code attribute, all required by Python
choices.why: None of those is required, and most classes have none of them.

prompt: What is the test for whether your own class is worth defining?
hint: It is about somebody else.

choices.text: Whether the message is longer than one line
choices.why: A long message is still a message.

choices.text: Whether the standard library has a class with the same name
choices.why: Collisions are not the question.

choices.text: Whether a caller might want to catch exactly your failure
choices.why: Right — a script nobody catches needs `ValueError` and nothing more.

choices.text: Whether the failure happens more than once in your code
choices.why: Frequency says nothing about who catches it.

prompt: Why give a package one base class with the specific ones below it?
hint: Two kinds of caller.

choices.text: To make the messages consistent
choices.why: The messages are whatever you write.

choices.text: So the linter can find them
choices.why: Nothing looks for them.

choices.text: So a caller can catch all of them, or just one
choices.why: Right — the hierarchy from the first section, built for your code.

choices.text: Because Python requires a base class per module
choices.why: Nothing requires it.

prompt: Why call `super().__init__(message)` in your own exception's `__init__`?
hint: A log prints something.

choices.text: So the class can be raised
choices.why: It can be raised regardless.

choices.text: So the message reaches `str(e)`
choices.why: Right — otherwise a log prints a blank line.

choices.text: So `except` can match it
choices.why: Matching is by class, and unaffected.

choices.text: So the traceback has line numbers
choices.why: The traceback is built either way.

prompt: Why not inherit from `BaseException`?
hint: Think about where it lands in the tree.

choices.text: It has no message argument
choices.why: It takes one.

choices.text: It would sit outside every `except Exception` anybody wrote
choices.why: Right — beside `KeyboardInterrupt`, where nothing ordinary catches it.

choices.text: It is being removed from the language, and a subclass of it will stop working
choices.why: It is not going anywhere.

choices.text: It is an abstract class and cannot be subclassed, so the class statement itself fails
choices.why: It can be, which is the hazard.

prompt: What is wrong with `if exists(path):` before `open(path)`?
hint: Two moments, and something between them.

choices.text: `exists` answers `True` for a directory as well, so the open fails on those anyway
choices.why: It does, and that is a different complaint.

choices.text: `open` never raises when the file exists, so the check makes the handler unnecessary
choices.why: It can raise for permission, among others.

choices.text: `exists` is slower than `open`
choices.why: The cost is not the argument.

choices.text: The file might change between the check and the open
choices.why: Right — so you needed the `except` anyway.

prompt: Which values deserve an `if` rather than a `try`?
hint: The ones that cannot change under you.

choices.text: Your own, in memory
choices.why: Right — nobody writes a `try` to find out whether a list is empty.

choices.text: Another process's output
choices.why: Also outside your program.

choices.text: A file's contents
choices.why: That belongs to the world.

choices.text: A network response
choices.why: The same, and more so.

prompt: `config["port"]` in a `try` with a `KeyError` handler giving 5432. What is shorter?
hint: The standard library already has the forgiving version.

choices.text: `config.setdefault("port")`
choices.why: That writes into the dictionary, which is more than was asked.

choices.text: `config.keys()["port"]`
choices.why: `keys()` is not indexable, and this is not a lookup.

choices.text: `config["port"] or 5432`
choices.why: That still raises when the key is missing.

choices.text: `config.get("port", 5432)`
choices.why: Right — and `.pop` and `next(it, None)` are the same idea.

prompt: Which is usually faster in the case that normally succeeds?
hint: One of them pays on every call.

choices.text: Neither; they compile to the same thing
choices.why: They do not.

choices.text: The `if`
choices.why: It costs a lookup every time, including the many successful ones.

choices.text: It depends on the size of the file
choices.why: Size is not what is being compared.

choices.text: The `try`
choices.why: Right — the exception costs only when it happens.

prompt: What does the acronym stand for, and what is the rule under it?
hint: Forgiveness, and whose values you are asking about.

choices.text: Errors are fatal — prefer permission to forgiveness
choices.why: That is the acronym reversed.

choices.text: Every argument should first be validated — check before every use, without exception
choices.why: That is the style this section argues against.

choices.text: Easier to ask forgiveness than permission — ask about your own values, try the world's
choices.why: Right — the check has a race in it and the try does not.

choices.text: Exceptions are for flow control — raise one wherever a branch would do, and catch it above
choices.why: Raising instead of branching is not what this says.

prompt: `int("abc")` raises what?
hint: The type was right and the value was not.

choices.text: `ValueError`
choices.why: Right — and the message shows the string it could not read.

choices.text: `SyntaxError`
choices.why: That is about the source code, not the data.

choices.text: `TypeError`
choices.why: A string is exactly what `int` accepts.

choices.text: `AttributeError`
choices.why: Nothing was looked up on an object.

prompt: `len(5)` raises what, and whose bug is it usually?
hint: One of the two classes is almost always yours.

choices.text: `TypeError`, and usually yours
choices.why: Right — catching it is rarely the answer; the traceback is.

choices.text: `ValueError`, and usually the data's
choices.why: The value is fine; the type is not.

choices.text: `AttributeError`, and usually yours
choices.why: `len` is a function, not an attribute lookup.

choices.text: `TypeError`, and usually the data's
choices.why: Data rarely arrives as the wrong Python type.

prompt: `KeyError: 'port'` — what else does the message tell you?
hint: Look at how much is there.

choices.text: The line of your file
choices.why: That is the traceback, not the message.

choices.text: Which dictionary it was
choices.why: It does not name the dictionary.

choices.text: Nothing else
choices.why: Right — the key is the whole message, which confuses people once.

choices.text: The keys that DO exist
choices.why: It lists nothing.

prompt: `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'strip'` means what?
hint: One value was not what you thought.

choices.text: The object has a typo in its attribute name
choices.why: That is the other AttributeError, with a real object.

choices.text: You called a method on the class instead of on an instance of it, so `self` was never filled in
choices.why: That gives a different message.

choices.text: Something returned `None` and you used it as if it had not
choices.why: Right — and the question is which line produced the `None`.

choices.text: `strip` was removed from strings in this version of Python, so the call is out of date
choices.why: It is still there.

prompt: `except OSError` covers which family?
hint: The filesystem and the operating system.

choices.text: `KeyError` and `IndexError`
choices.why: Those are `LookupError`.

choices.text: Every exception a file operation can raise, including `UnicodeDecodeError`
choices.why: That one is a `ValueError`, which `except OSError` does not catch.

choices.text: `FileNotFoundError`, `PermissionError`, `IsADirectoryError`
choices.why: Right — which is the clause to write when your answer is the same for each.

choices.text: `ValueError` and `TypeError`
choices.why: Neither is about the system.

prompt: Which end of a traceback do you read first?
hint: The error is at one end.

choices.text: The middle, where the library calls begin
choices.why: Nothing marks a middle.

choices.text: Whichever line is longest
choices.why: Length says nothing.

choices.text: The top
choices.why: That is how you got there, which matters second.

choices.text: The bottom
choices.why: Right — then upwards to the first line that is yours.

prompt: Which clause runs whether or not the block raised?
hint: Cleanup.

choices.text: `try`
choices.why: That is the block itself.

choices.text: `else`
choices.why: That runs only when nothing raised.

choices.text: `except`
choices.why: That runs only when something did.

choices.text: `finally`
choices.why: Right — including on a `return`.

prompt: Which exception is the wrong one to catch, ever?
hint: Two classes sit outside `Exception` for a reason.

choices.text: `KeyError`, because `.get` exists
choices.why: `.get` is nicer and catching is not wrong.

choices.text: `OSError`, because the filesystem is unpredictable
choices.why: That is the case for catching it.

choices.text: `ValueError`, because the data is not yours to fix
choices.why: Catching it to say which field is exactly right.

choices.text: `KeyboardInterrupt`, by writing a bare `except:`
choices.why: Right — and `SystemExit` with it.

prompt: Keep the original failure as the cause of yours: `raise ConfigError(...) ______ e`
hint: Four letters.

prompt: A handler that does `pass` needs what, if it is genuinely right?
hint: Somebody will read this in six months.

choices.text: Nothing at all; a `pass` in a handler is self-explanatory to whoever reads it
choices.why: It explains that nothing happens, not why that is right.

choices.text: A `finally` beside it
choices.why: Cleanup is a different question.

choices.text: A log line at debug level, so the failure is at least recorded somewhere
choices.why: Better than nothing and still not why.

choices.text: A comment naming the class and saying why the silence is safe
choices.why: Right — and without it, it reads as a bug somebody hid.

prompt: `None.strip()`. Which class?
hint: The value was `None`.

choices.text: `NameError`
choices.why: `None` is defined.

choices.text: `AttributeError`
choices.why: Right — and the `NoneType` in the message is the clue.

choices.text: `ValueError`
choices.why: Nothing was parsed.

choices.text: `TypeError`
choices.why: Close in spirit, and the message would name a type mismatch instead.

prompt: How big should the `try` block be?
hint: As small as one thing.

choices.text: Around everything that touches the same file
choices.why: Several of those can raise the same class.

choices.text: Around the line that fails, and nothing else
choices.why: Right — a wide `try` catches something it was never meant to see.

choices.text: Around the whole function, so nothing escapes
choices.why: Then the handler answers for anything.

choices.text: Whatever fits between the blank lines
choices.why: Layout is not the test.

prompt: Two clauses, `except OSError` then `except FileNotFoundError`. What is the second?
hint: Order decides.

choices.text: A second chance if the first re-raises
choices.why: Nothing re-raises here.

choices.text: The one that runs for a missing file
choices.why: The base class above it took that case.

choices.text: A syntax error
choices.why: It is accepted.

choices.text: Unreachable
choices.why: Right — and nothing warns you.

prompt: Which is the one-line version of `try`/`finally` for a file?
hint: Lesson 9 is built on it.

choices.text: `with open(path) as f:`
choices.why: Right — and anything with a lock or a connection has one.

choices.text: `open(path).close()`
choices.why: That opens and closes it, having read nothing.

choices.text: `try: open(path)`
choices.why: That is the half without the cleanup.

choices.text: `f = open(path); del f`
choices.why: Deleting the name is not closing the file.

prompt: The clause for code that must run only when nothing raised: `______:`
hint: Four letters.

prompt: A library reads configuration. What should it raise on a bad file?
hint: Think about what the program above it wants to say.

choices.text: `Exception`
choices.why: Catchable only by catching everything.

choices.text: `SystemExit`
choices.why: A library deciding to end the program is not its call.

choices.text: `ValueError`
choices.why: Indistinguishable from any other value problem inside it.

choices.text: Its own `ConfigError`
choices.why: Right — so the caller can exit 2 for that and nothing else.

prompt: When is NOT catching an exception the correct decision?
hint: Ask what you would do about it.

choices.text: When there is nothing useful you would do here
choices.why: Right — the code above might know, and the traceback certainly does.

choices.text: When the function has no `finally`
choices.why: Cleanup is unrelated.

choices.text: When the exception is rare
choices.why: Rarity is not the question.

choices.text: When a test already covers it
choices.why: A test does not handle a failure in production.

prompt: What does `raise e` lose that a bare `raise` keeps?
hint: Something about where it came from.

choices.text: The class
choices.why: Also unchanged.

choices.text: The original traceback
choices.why: Right — the bare form re-raises what you caught, intact.

choices.text: The message
choices.why: The message survives both.

choices.text: The chaining to the cause
choices.why: That is what `from` controls.
